solutions.text: The Peace of Westphalia was signed in 1648 and, as part of the settlement that ended the Thirty Years' War, Spain finally recognised the independence of the Dutch Republic after the Eighty Years' War. The Spanish crown for Philip V, grandson of Louis XIV, was settled a lifetime later at Utrecht in 1713, and the Holy Roman Empire survived Westphalia until 1806.

The War of the Spanish Succession ended with the Peace of Utrecht of 1713, which recognised Philip V as king of Spain on condition that the French and Spanish crowns never unite. The other treaties close different conflicts: Westphalia (1648) the Thirty Years' War, Ryswick (1697) the Nine Years' War, Nystad (1721) the Great Northern War and Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) the War of the Austrian Succession.

In the October Revolution of 1917 (November by the Western calendar) the Bolsheviks under Lenin overthrew Kerensky's Provisional Government. Nicholas II had already been deposed by the February Revolution, the Constituent Assembly was elected only after the seizure of power and dissolved in January 1918, and Kolchak's White armies were defeated in the civil war of 1919 to 1920.

The Glorious Revolution of 1688 deposed the Catholic king James II and gave the throne jointly to William of Orange and his wife Mary, James II's own daughter, with the Bill of Rights of 1689 confirming parliamentary supremacy. The execution of Charles I and the republic belong to the Civil War of the 1640s, Charles II's return to the restoration of 1660, and the Hanoverian succession to 1714.

The Meiji Restoration of 1868 returned supreme power to the emperor and abolished the Tokugawa shogunate, whose last shogun was Yoshinobu. Meiji is the name of the era rather than the city, since Edo was renamed Tokyo; the first shogunate under Minamoto no Yoritomo dates from the twelfth century; and the end of the Qing dynasty and the republic of Sun Yat-sen belong to China in 1912.

The Treaty of Trianon, signed in June 1920, was imposed on Hungary, which lost about two thirds of its territory and population. The pattern across the Paris settlement is worth memorising: Versailles for Germany, Saint-Germain for Austria, Neuilly for Bulgaria, Trianon for Hungary and Sevres for the Ottoman Empire.

Constantinople fell to Mehmed II on 29 May 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire. Suleiman's siege of Vienna in 1529 failed, as did the second siege of 1683; Baghdad was sacked by the Mongols in 1258 and taken by the Ottomans only in 1534; Belgrade fell in 1521; and Rhodes was captured by Suleiman in 1522, so the knights did not keep it.

Francisco Pizarro seized the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532 and had him executed in 1533. It was Cortes, not Balboa, who took the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan in 1521; Velazquez stayed in Cuba as governor; and Magellan died in the Philippines before his expedition completed the first circumnavigation.

At the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, convened by Bismarck, the powers recognised the Congo claims of King Leopold II, who then ruled the Congo Free State as his personal possession rather than a Belgian colony. Belgium annexed the territory only in 1908, after international protest at the atrocities of his regime; his father Leopold I had no part in the Congo.

German reunification took effect on 3 October 1990, when the German Democratic Republic acceded to the Federal Republic under the Unification Treaty, after the Two Plus Four settlement with the four former occupying powers. The opening of the Wall on 9 November 1989 was only the prelude, both German states had been UN members together since 1973, and the Warsaw Pact was dissolved after unification.

Midnight's Children is Salman Rushdie's 1981 novel, winner of the Booker Prize and later voted the Booker of Bookers, about children born in the first hour of Indian independence. Naipaul, Roy, Ishiguro and Mistry are the plausible alternatives, but the birth-moment-of-the-nation premise belongs to Rushdie.

The Tale of Genji was written in the early eleventh century by Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court, and is often called the world's first novel. The compilation of lists and palace observations is Sei Shonagon's Pillow Book, and Basho's poetic travel diaries are seventeenth-century works.

The line about the best and worst of times opens A Tale of Two Cities of 1859, set in London and Paris in the age of the French Revolution. All five titles are Dickens novels, so the item turns purely on knowing which book carries which opening.

L'Etranger, the 1942 novel narrated without emotion by Meursault, is by Albert Camus, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957. Sartre is the tempting confusion because of their shared existentialism, but Sartre wrote Nausea, and Beckett and Ionesco are chiefly dramatists.

Ulysses, published in 1922, is James Joyce's transposition of the Odyssey onto a single Dublin day, 16 June 1904, seen through Leopold Bloom. Virginia Woolf is the natural trap, since her Mrs Dalloway is also a one-day novel by a modernist of the same generation.

Things Fall Apart is Chinua Achebe's 1958 debut novel, centred on the Igbo villager Okonkwo whose world collapses under colonial rule, and a foundation stone of modern African literature. Wole Soyinka was indeed the first African winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature, but he is a playwright, and Ngugi, Gordimer and Coetzee are authors of other books.

Gilgamesh, the legendary king of Uruk, is the hero of the Epic of Gilgamesh, the oldest surviving major work of narrative literature, from ancient Mesopotamia. The Aeneid follows Aeneas, Beowulf the hero of the Geats, the Ramayana prince Rama, and the Song of Roland Charlemagne's rearguard at Roncevaux.

Crime and Punishment (1866), The Idiot (1869) and The Brothers Karamazov (1880) are all novels of Fyodor Dostoevsky. Tolstoy wrote War and Peace and Anna Karenina, Turgenev is known for Fathers and Sons, Gogol wrote Dead Souls, and Eugene Onegin is Pushkin's novel in verse.

Only states may be parties in cases before the International Court of Justice, the United Nations' principal judicial organ, while the International Criminal Court, set up by the Rome Statute in force since 2002, prosecutes individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression. The two are often confused: the ICC is independent of the UN, not its judicial organ, and the ICJ cannot hand down sentences.

Long settled practice, confirmed by the International Court of Justice, treats a permanent member's abstention, like an absence, as not a veto: the resolution passes if it wins nine of fifteen votes with no permanent member voting against. Requiring the concurring votes of all five misreads the Charter and would have blocked most resolutions ever adopted.

The IMF lends short and medium term to members facing balance-of-payments difficulties, while the World Bank finances long-term development and poverty-reduction projects such as infrastructure. The wrong options simply swap the two mandates, and the WTO, although closely linked to the UN, is not one of its specialized agencies and has no exchange-rate role.

Every peacekeeping operation is authorised by a Security Council resolution and manned by national contingents voluntarily contributed by member states, since the UN has no standing army. The guiding principles are consent of the parties, impartiality and force only in self-defence and defence of the mandate, and contingents serve under UN operational command, not their own governments.

The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 protect wounded and sick combatants, the shipwrecked, prisoners of war and civilians, and with 196 states parties they are the most universally ratified treaties in existence. They protect people rather than regulate weapons (that is Hague law), they apply to every armed conflict whether or not war was formally declared, and no tribunal sentences states.

Article 5 has been invoked only once, after the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001. Each ally then decides for itself what action to take, including the use of armed force, since the clause requires assistance as each deems necessary rather than an automatic identical military response, and Korea, the Cuban missile crisis and the Falklands never triggered it.

Under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, a signature given subject to ratification does not yet make the state a party, but Article 18 already obliges it to refrain from acts that would defeat the treaty's object and purpose. Ratification is the act that expresses consent to be bound, so the fully-binding-at-signature reading confuses the two steps.

Article 25 of the UN Charter obliges members to accept and carry out the Security Council's decisions, which can bind all states, while General Assembly resolutions on peace and security are recommendations with political rather than legal force. The Assembly cannot authorise enforcement action to work around a veto, and no domestic constitution overrides a binding Council decision.

Article 127 TFEU makes price stability the primary objective of the European System of Central Banks, and support for the Union's other economic policies is allowed only without prejudice to that goal. The treaties forbid the ECB and national central banks from financing government deficits, and interest-rate setting is centralised, so euro-area national banks do not control their own rates.

Raising policy rates makes credit dearer, cools demand and eases inflationary pressure, and the higher yields tend to attract capital inflows that strengthen the currency. The reversed options fail on mechanism: borrowing becomes more expensive rather than cheaper, savers earn more rather than less, and no increase in tax revenue cancels the public deficit one for one.

GDP is territorial: the output of the Lombardy plant counts in Italian GDP whatever the nationality of its owners. GNI follows residents' income, so the profits paid to shareholders in Japan enter Japan's gross national income; counting the production as Japanese GDP, or excluding it from Italian accounts, confuses where production happens with who owns it.

The constructive vote of no confidence lets the Bundestag remove a Chancellor only by electing a successor at the same time with the majority of all its members, a safeguard adopted after the Weimar experience. Dismissal by a simple majority of those present, or automatic dissolution of parliament, is precisely the instability the Basic Law was designed to prevent.

The Maastricht convergence criteria require inflation no more than 1.5 percentage points above that of the three best-performing member states and at least two years in the exchange-rate mechanism without devaluation. The other figures are inventions: the deficit reference is 3 percent of GDP, the debt reference 60 percent, and euro adoption follows the criteria rather than arriving automatically with EU membership.

Progressive taxation works slab by slab: once income crosses into a higher bracket, only the portion above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate, and the tax on the lower slabs is unchanged. Taxing the whole income at the new rate is the classic mistake, and in this setup a pay rise can never reduce the total bill.

New Zealand's Electoral Act of 1893 made it the first self-governing country to give women the vote in parliamentary elections. The British franchise of 1918 was partial, covering mainly women over thirty with property qualifications, full equality came in 1928, and Swiss women waited until 1971 for the federal vote.

First past the post gives the seat to the candidate with the most votes in the constituency, a simple plurality, even far short of half the votes cast. Second rounds between the top two belong to majority runoff systems, and neither a threshold among registered voters nor the national popular vote decides any seat.

Confirmatory referendums under Article 138 have no turnout quorum: a simple majority of valid votes cast decides, so the amendment is rejected if most of those voting are against it. The 2020 seat-cut reform passed with about 70 percent yes on roughly 51 percent turnout; the rule that half the electorate must vote belongs to Article 75 abrogative referendums.

Under Article 138, a constitutional law approved without a two-thirds majority in the second vote is suspended if one fifth of a chamber, five regional councils or 500,000 voters request a referendum; in 2016 the minority did so, and the No side won with about 59 percent, forcing Renzi's resignation. No rule makes a popular vote compulsory: with a two-thirds majority the law is promulgated directly.

Presidential acts in Italy are valid only with the counter-signature of the proposing ministers (Article 89), and the President may not dissolve the Chambers in the last six months of the presidential term except in the recognised narrow cases (Article 88). Italy is parliamentary: the government answers to Parliament, so the head of state cannot dismiss the Prime Minister at will.

Italian constitutional review is incidental and centralised: the ordinary judge who doubts a statute's constitutionality stays the proceedings and refers the question to the Constitutional Court, the only body that may declare a law unconstitutional with effect for everyone. Direct disapplication is the technique reserved for conflicting EU law, which judges of any level must set aside.

Article 75 makes an abrogative referendum valid only if at least half of those entitled to vote actually take part. In June 2025 turnout was about 30 percent, so all five questions, citizenship included, failed despite the Yes majorities among those who voted; counting valid votes alone ignores the quorum that sank the ballots.

The 2001 reform of Title V inverted the logic of Article 117: the Constitution lists the State's exclusive matters and the concurrent ones, and all matters not listed belong to the regions as residual competence. Criminal law and the organisation of the judiciary are firmly among the State's exclusive powers, so the option treating criminal law as concurrent misreads the list.

On 1 July 1858 the Linnean Society of London heard Darwin's and Wallace's papers on natural selection read together, presented by Joseph Hooker and Charles Lyell: Darwin stayed away, mourning his young son, and Wallace was still in the Malay Archipelago, so neither author was present. On the Origin of Species followed in November 1859, more than half a century before Wallace's death in 1913.

Newton had developed the method of fluxions around 1665 to 1666 but kept it unpublished, while Leibniz issued the first printed account of differential calculus in the Acta Eruditorum in 1684; historians agree the two worked independently. The Royal Society's 1712 report awarded priority to Newton, whose own account appeared only in 1704, and the commission could hardly be neutral since he presided over the Society.

Mendel's laws were rediscovered and republished in 1900 by three botanists working independently: Hugo de Vries in the Netherlands, Carl Correns in Germany and Erich von Tschermak in Austria, each citing the 1866 paper. The other trios belong to DNA structure (Watson, Crick, Wilkins), bacteriology (Koch, Ehrlich, Behring) and fruit-fly chromosome mapping (Morgan, Sturtevant, Bridges).

The 1887 experiment in Cleveland split a light beam with an interferometer and found no measurable difference in light speed with Earth's direction of motion, a null result that undermined the luminiferous aether and paved the way to Einstein's special relativity of 1905. Michelson's 1907 Nobel honoured the interferometer and precision optics, and the oil-drop electron measurement was Millikan's.

Rosalind Franklin died of cancer in April 1958, aged 37, and Nobel statutes exclude posthumous awards, so she could not share the 1962 prize given to Watson, Crick and Wilkins. The story of a principled refusal is a myth, and the 1962 chemistry prize went to Perutz and Kendrew for protein structure, not to Franklin.

Hershey and Chase found that only the phosphorus-32 label, tagging DNA, entered the infected bacteria, while the sulphur-35-labelled protein coats were sheared off outside the cells: DNA, not protein, carries the phage's heredity. The transforming principle extracted from heat-killed bacteria belongs to Griffith and Avery, and X-ray diffraction belongs to the later DNA structure story.

Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 but could not purify it; the Oxford team led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain did, running the first clinical trials in 1941, and the three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Lister's antiseptic was carbolic acid, Ehrlich's magic bullet was Salvarsan against syphilis, and Waksman's 1952 prize was for streptomycin.

Tokyo is 9 hours ahead of UTC and Los Angeles 8 hours behind, so 17 hours come off the naive total. Departure at 08:00 Monday Tokyo time is 23:00 Sunday UTC; after the 10-hour flight it is 09:00 Monday UTC, which is 01:00 Monday in Los Angeles. Simply adding 8 plus 10 hours to reach 18:00 Monday ignores both zones, and the eastward crossing gains hours rather than costing a day.

Ships leave the Black Sea through the Bosporus into the Sea of Marmara and then through the Dardanelles into the Aegean. The Strait of Hormuz joins the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, not the Red Sea; the Suez Canal links the Red Sea to the Mediterranean; and the Panama Canal joins the Pacific to the Caribbean side of the Atlantic.

The Danube flows through four national capitals, Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade, more than any other river. The Volga, Europe's longest river, empties into the Caspian Sea and serves no foreign capitals, and the Amazon, not the Nile, carries by far the greatest volume of water to the sea.

Mont Blanc, about 4808 m on the French-Italian border in the Alps, is the highest mountain of the European Union. Elbrus at 5642 m tops geographic Europe only under the Caucasus definition and stands in Russia, outside the EU, while Etna, Europe's tallest active volcano, reaches only about 3350 m.

Switzerland's largest city is Zurich, but the federal government sits in Bern, the de facto capital. The same capital-versus-largest-city split appears in the other options: Canberra rather than Sydney for Australia, Ankara rather than Istanbul for Turkey, Ottawa rather than Toronto for Canada, and Brasilia, capital since 1960, rather than Rio de Janeiro for Brazil.

Malta, which joined the EU in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2008, is the only state listed that is both a full member and a euro user. San Marino, Andorra and Vatican City use the euro only through monetary agreements without membership, and Liechtenstein, an EEA member through EFTA, keeps the Swiss franc.

Martin Luther issued the Ninety-five Theses at Wittenberg in October 1517 against the sale of indulgences. Calvin led the Reformation at Geneva, Zwingli at Zurich, Henry VIII's break with Rome came through the Act of Supremacy of 1534, and Jan Hus was burned at the Council of Constance in 1415, a century before Luther.

The war of every man against every man, and life as solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short, is Thomas Hobbes's description of the state of nature in Leviathan of 1651, written in the shadow of the English Civil War. Locke argued for natural rights and limited government, Rousseau imagined a far more benign state of nature, and More and Machiavelli wrote other works entirely.

The Bhagavad Gita is the Sanskrit dialogue embedded in the Mahabharata in which the god Krishna instructs the warrior Arjuna on duty before the battle of Kurukshetra. The rival descriptions point to the Ramayana, the Rigveda, the Arthashastra attributed to Kautilya and the Upanishads.

The Guru Granth Sahib is the principal scripture of Sikhism, honoured by Sikhs as the eternal living guru, its core the hymns of Guru Nanak and his successors. The corresponding texts are the Vedas for Hinduism, the Tripitaka for Buddhism, the Agamas for Jainism and the Avesta for Zoroastrianism.

The Critique of Pure Reason of 1781, which delimits what human reason can and cannot know, is Immanuel Kant's work. Kant credited Hume's scepticism with waking him from his dogmatic slumber; Descartes wrote the Meditations, Spinoza the Ethics and Hegel the Phenomenology of Spirit.

The WHO Pandemic Agreement was adopted by consensus at the 78th World Health Assembly in Geneva on 20 May 2025, the first such accord shaped by the COVID-19 pandemic. It is not yet in force, since entry into force requires 60 ratifications; it was negotiated at the WHO, not the UN General Assembly or the G20, and it supplements rather than replaces the International Health Regulations.

The obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models first became applicable on 2 August 2025. The Act entered into force on 1 August 2024, but its rules bite in stages: prohibitions and the AI literacy duty from 2 February 2025, then the general-purpose AI model rules, with the high-risk system obligations last in the timetable, so only 2025 matches the milestone asked.

notes: All 60 derived answers agree with the stored keys after re-derivation and fact-checking; no disagreements.

Q60: the stored explanation cites a Digital Omnibus adopted in July 2026 postponing the high-risk obligations to 2027-2028; that late-2026 legislative step could not be independently verified, but the derived answer (2025) rests on the Act's original staged timetable and is unaffected.

Q59 and Q39 involve 2025 events; both match the settled public record (WHA78 consensus adoption on 20 May 2025; the five Italian abrogative referendums of 8-9 June 2025 all failing on the 50 percent turnout quorum).
Q51: the answer holds under either convention on Europe's highest peak, since Elbrus lies in Russia and outside the EU, leaving Mont Blanc as the highest EU summit.
